sec.title: Aims
sec.p: To examine the effects of administering detemir and glargine insulin on the detection of endogenous C-peptide and insulin levels.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: This study enrolled 69 patients with type 2 diabetes (T2DM) who use long-acting insulin therapy. Fasting and postprandial blood glucose (BG), C-peptide, and insulin were detected for two consecutive mornings. Fasting and postprandial C-peptide/BG and insulin/BG were then compared between groups treated with or without detemir and glargine insulin the night before. Thirty patients with type 1 diabetes (T1DM) verified the results.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: In patients with T2DM, compared with the results obtained from the group that did not administer insulin the night prior to testing, fasting C-peptide (CP0h), CP0h/fasting blood glucose (FBG), fasting insulin (INS0h), and INS0h /FBG were decreased with the use of detemir. Similarly, CP0h and CP0h/FBG were decreased in the group that had glargine administered the night before testing. However, there was no significant difference in INS0h and INS0h/FBG with and without the use of glargine insulin. The use of long-acting insulin had no effect on the postprandial C-peptide/PBG and postprandial insulin/PBG. In patients with T1DM, CP0h/FBG was hardly detected and had no difference between glargine and detemir groups. However, after using detemir the night before, the INS0h/FBG was hardly detected; insulin could be detected in the glargine group.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: Exclusive dependence on C-peptide levels as a primary metric for the direct evaluation of pancreatic function under insulin therapy is insufficient. A comprehensive assessment necessitates due consideration of the insulin type employed for quantifying insulin and C-peptide concentrations.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: One in ten adults worldwide live with diabetes according to the International Diabetes Federation diabetes atlas 11th edition. In China, diabetes-associated healthcare expenditure reached 165.3 billion dollars in 2021 (https://diabetesatlas.org/). In recent years, new types of oral hypoglycemic agents and exogenous insulins have been developed. Exogenous insulin is the most important therapy for patients with type 1 diabetes, as well as for patients with type 2 diabetes and pancreatic islet dysfunction. However, accurately evaluating pancreatic islet function and selecting an appropriate therapy for these patients remains a challenge.

Insulin (INS) is an endogenous peptide hormone with important physiological roles in glucose regulation and anabolism [1]. In pancreatic β cells, proinsulin is processed by proteases and carboxypeptidase into C-peptide (CP) and mature insulin, two peptides with equal gram molecular concentrations [2]. CP is considered the superior marker with which to evaluate pancreatic islet function due to its longer half-life [3]. In the context of a person with diabetes reliant on exogenous insulin, it is standard clinical practice to measure CP levels as a means to appraise the genuine functioning of pancreatic beta cells. This practice assumes paramount significance owing to the potential influence of exogenous insulin administration on the precise determination of endogenous insulin levels [4–6]. However, some studies have indicated that exogenous insulins inhibit the secretion of endogenous insulin [7, 8], particularly if long-acting insulin is administered the night before testing [9]. Consequently, in such a situation, there is a likelihood that the secretion of CP would also be suppressed. Therefore, employing CP levels as a means to evaluate pancreatic function carries a potential risk of underestimating the actual pancreatic function. Accurately evaluating pancreatic islet function and selecting an appropriate therapy for these patients who use long-acting insulin therapy remains a challenge. Despite the widespread use of long-acting insulin, there has been little research conducted on the evaluation of plasma insulin and CP levels in the context of long-acting insulin application.
Therefore, in the current study, we explored how the application of long-acting insulin affects the detection of endogenous C-peptide and insulin levels.

sec.title: Study design
sec.p: We conducted a study involving patients diagnosed with type 2 diabetes and type 1 diabetes, recruited from the Department of Endocrinology and Metabolic Management Center at the First People’s Hospital of Yunnan Province. Inclusion criteria were as follows: (1) type 2 diabetes and type 1 diabetes patients conforming to the diagnostic criteria specified in the 2021 American Diabetes Association (ADA) guidelines. (2) Utilization of detemir or glargine insulin as a bedtime regimen. (3) No concurrent usage of sulphonylureas, dipeptidyl peptidase-4 inhibitors (DPP-4I), or glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RA). (4) Exclusive use of metformin immediate-release tablets as an insulin sensitizer during mealtime treatment. (5) Fasting insulin levels not exceeding 40 μU/mL, and postprandial insulin levels not exceeding 130 μU/mL at 2 h after a 100 g steamed bun meal, to minimize the confounding effect caused by insulin resistance. (6) In the context of bedtime basal insulin therapy, the ideal fasting blood glucose (FBG) levels should fall within the range of 4 mmol/L to 9 mmol/L. Patients with alternative types of diabetes, those taking medications affecting glucose levels (e.g., diuretics, glucocorticoids, and euthyrox), individuals with abnormal thyroid, renal, or liver function, as well as those with gout, tumors, or infections were excluded from the study. Blood glucose, INS, and CP levels were measured in all participants during fasting and two hours after consuming 100 g of flour steamed bread for two consecutive days. Patients previously treated with detemir insulin were assigned to the detemir group, while those previously treated with glargine insulin were assigned to the glargine group. The patients’ long-acting insulin (detemir or glargine) was administered at 11 pm on the night preceding the first blood collection, and subsequently discontinued for the rest of the study. Fasting blood samples were taken between 7 and 8 AM, and postprandial blood samples were obtained between 9 and 10 AM. On the day of blood sampling, all oral medications and insulin treatments were withheld in the morning.

This study was approved by the Ethics Committee of the First People’s Hospital of Yunnan Province. All patients signed an informed consent form. The Chinese clinical trial registry number—a primary registry of International Clinical Trial Registry Clinical Platform, World Health Organization—is chiCTR1800014910.

sec.title: Clinical parameters
sec.p: Clinical parameters including age, gender, type of diabetes, and liver and renal function were collected from electronic medical records provided by our hospital. FBG and postprandial blood glucose (PBG) levels were analyzed by Abbott Biochemistry Analyzer c16000, and CP, and INS were analyzed by electrochemiluminescence immunoassay (ECLIA) (Cobas e601, Roche). Antibody specificity serves as the cornerstone for the accurate differentiation and quantitative detection of insulin and C-peptide in ECLIA. The antigen-binding sites of insulin-specific antibodies are designed to achieve perfect complementarity with the specific three-dimensional structures on the surface of insulin molecules. Similarly, antibodies targeting C-peptide exclusively recognize the unique spatial conformations of C-peptide molecules. By employing highly specific monoclonal antibodies, modern ECLIA kits minimize cross-reactivity with proinsulin to an extremely low level, thereby ensuring highly specific detection and effectively avoiding non-specific interference. INS/weight represented the insulin injection dose per kilogram. We used CP0h/FBG, CP2h/PBG, INS0h/FBG, INS2h/PBG to correct for the bias of unstable glucose.

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: Data with normal distribution are presented as mean ± standard deviation or as interquartile range for skewed distributions. SPSS (version 20.0) was employed to analyze the data. Differences between groups were appropriately analyzed by t-test and Chi-square test. Multivariable logistic regression was used to analyze correlations. All P-values were two-tailed distributions, and P < 0.05 was considered statistically significant.

sec.title: Effects of exogenous insulin on the detection of endogenous C-peptide and insulin in patients with type 2 diabetes
sec.p:
Table 2 presents the levels of glucose, CP, and endogenous insulin with and without the use of glargine or detemir insulin the night prior to testing. Overall, CP0h and CP2h were significantly decreased with the use of glargine the night before. On the other hand, there were no differences with fasting and postprandial insulin. When detemir insulin was administered the night before testing, fasting insulin and C-peptide were significantly lower than that without detemir insulin use the prior night, but postprandial insulin and C-peptide showed no difference between the two groups. We then used C-peptide/glucose and insulin/glucose ratios to minimize the bias of fluctuating glucose levels. As illustrated in Fig. 1, the pre-test use of glargine or detemir decreased CP0h/FBG compared to the group that did not receive insulin. Interestingly, INS0h/FBG decreased with the use of detemir insulin but not glargine compared to the no insulin group (Fig. 1). Moreover, CP2h/PBG and INS2h/PBG were not different between any of the groups.Fig. 1

sec.title: Correlation of endogenous C-peptide and insulin with and without administration of exogenous insulin
sec.p:
A multiple linear regression analysis revealed that fasting C-peptide levels after glargine or detemir administration positively correlated with fasting C-peptide without insulin (Fig. 2). Similarly, fasting insulin levels after glargine or detemir positively correlated with fasting insulin levels in the group that did not receive insulin the night prior to testing. Overall, fasting insulin in the glargine treatment group correlated the most with the untreated group. We could potentially utilize a regression equation to approximate the fasting C-peptide and insulin levels of a patient without administering insulin, based on their fasting C-peptide and insulin levels with insulin.Fig. 2
Correlations of endogenous C-peptide and insulin with and without exogenous insulins. INS0h fasting blood insulin, CP0h fasting blood C-peptide. All P-values were two-tailed distributions, and P < 0.05 was considered statistically significant

sec.title: The predictive ROC curve of fasting C-peptide levels after treatment with glargine and detemir when true C-peptide is below normal levels
sec.p:
Patients with fasting C-peptide levels less than or equal to 0.48 nmol/L, who were not treated with glargine and detemir, were categorized as the abnormal group, while the rest were categorized as the normal group. The risk of abnormal fasting C-peptide levels after treatment with glargine and detemir in predicting true fasting C-peptide levels was assessed by constructing ROC curves. The results (Fig. 3) showed that the areas under the ROC curves for predicting true C-peptide levels after treatment with glargine and detemir were 0.7768 and 0.8762, respectively (P < 0.001), with cutoff values of 0.4435 nmol/L (sensitivity 52.2%; specificity 93.3%) and 0.379 nmol/L (sensitivity 86.4%; specificity 76.8%).Fig. 3
The predictive ROC curve of fasting C-peptide levels after treatment with glargine and detemir when true C-peptide is below normal levels. CP0h fasting blood C-peptide

sec.title: Effects of exogenous insulin on the detection of endogenous C-peptide and insulin in patients with type 1 diabetes
sec.p:
To verify the above results, we detected the FBG, PBG, CP0h/FBG, CP2h/PBG, INS0h/FBG, and INS2h/PBG in patients with type 1 diabetes. Twenty patients of them used glargine insulin, and ten patients used detemir insulin (the demographic and clinical characteristics of them could be provided). As Fig. 4 shows, CP0h/FBG was hardly detected, and has no difference between glargine and detemir groups. However, after using detemir the night before, the INS0h/FBG was hardly detected; insulin could be detected in the glargine group.Fig. 4

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: The incidence and morbidity of type 2 diabetes has increased rapidly alongside modern lifestyle changes. The micro- and macrovascular complications of diabetes pose a heavy burden on health systems worldwide [10]. The management of type 2 diabetes includes lifestyle changes, patient education, oral hypoglycemic agents, and INS. Evaluating islet β-cell function is critical for selecting the appropriate type 2 diabetes therapy. The hyperinsulinemic-euglycemic clamping test is currently the gold standard for measuring islet β-cell function; however, this test is complex and expensive. Thus, the oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT) is an appropriate substitute [11].

In pancreatic β cells, proinsulin is processed by proteases and carboxypeptidase into CP and INS at equal gram molecular concentrations. CP is a single-chain linear peptide consisting of 31 amino acids, while insulin consists of two chains and contains a total of 51 amino acids [4]. Because of their equimolar production and release from the pancreas, the concentrations of endogenous insulin and C-peptide frequently correlate, although their plasma half-lives are different. The half-life of insulin is about 4 min due to its inactivation by insulinase in the liver and kidneys. Conversely, CP is rarely utilized by insulin target organs and does not undergo hepatic first-pass extraction; thus, its half-life is up to 30 min [9]. Therefore, fasting and postprandial C-peptide levels obtained from OGTT are more reliable.

The absolute plasma concentrations for both peptide hormones are in the low range (ng/mL) [12], and there are many factors that impact the detection of endogenous insulin and C-peptide. The first consideration is the blood glucose control status [13, 14]. Under normal physiological conditions, endogenous insulin and C-peptide secretion increase to balance an increase in glucose levels. However, patients with type 2 diabetes who receive exogenous insulin treatment experience β-cell islet dysfunction [15]. In clinical practice, patients often continue the use of their long-acting insulins the night before the steamed bun meal test to ensure stable and safe glucose levels. Given the potential interference of exogenous insulin on insulin detection, clinicians frequently rely on simultaneous measurement of CP levels as an alternative to INS levels when evaluating pancreatic function. However, the use of exogenous insulins can suppress the secretion of endogenous insulin, potentially resulting in an underestimation of pancreatic islet function [16]. If CP and INS are secreted in equimolar amounts, the use of exogenous insulin can lead to a reduction in endogenous C-peptide levels, raising questions about the appropriateness of relying solely on C-peptide levels for assessing pancreatic insulin function.

In the present study, we found that fasting C-peptide levels were decreased when long-acting insulin was used the night before compared to the no insulin group. Considering that blood glucose levels affect endogenous insulin and C-peptide secretion, to reduce the interference caused by blood glucose, we used the ratio of C-peptide and glucose to reduce the bias of glucose levels. Although the FBG was significantly lower with the use of insulin, CP0h/FBG was also decreased compared to the no insulin group. These results are similar to those reported by previous studies [7, 9] and indicate that exogenous insulin inhibits the secretion of endogenous CP0h. Therefore, it is our contention that assessing the basal secretion of pancreatic beta cells using fasting C-peptide levels in the context of basal insulin therapy is not ideal.

In the study, detemir also lowered fasting insulin levels at the same time, whereas fasting insulin levels did not differ much from true levels after glargine administration. The INS0h/FBG ratio also yielded similar outcomes. The important factor related to the detection of endogenous insulin is the testing method. Currently, ECLIA is one of the most popular methods to evaluate insulin levels. ECLIA is based on the combination of a specific insulin antibody and endogenous insulin [17]. However, studies have shown that exogenous insulin can cross-react with the antibody [18]. An in vitro study collected serum from healthy participants to evaluate the interference of exogenous short/intermediate/long-acting insulin on insulin detection via ECLIA. The results indicated that glargine insulin displayed a linear positive interference, and detemir had a linear negative interference [19]. Although glargine insulin inhibited endogenous insulin secretion in our study, similar to other results, the fasting insulin levels were not affected [12]. These results may be related to a positive interference of glargine on endogenous insulin testing. The reduction of fasting insulin levels by detemir was related to its inhibition of insulin secretion and negative interference with the assay.

To verify the results, we also evaluated the effect of exogenous insulins in patients with type 1 diabetes. Because endogenous insulin is absolutely deficient in people with type 1 diabetes, we could assume that the tested insulin is totally exogenous insulin. The results confirm our hypothesis; the tested glargine should be exogenous insulin, and detemir was hardly tested in the second morning. In other words, in the detemir group, the detected insulin was almost endogenous insulin (inhibited); in the glargine group, the detected insulin included endogenous insulin (inhibited) and glargine (Fig. 5).Fig. 5
Effects of exogenous detemir and glargine insulin on the detection of endogenous insulin. In detemir group, the detected insulin was almost endogenous insulin (inhibited). In glargine group, the detected insulin included endogenous insulin (inhibited) and glargine. INS0h fasting blood insulin

Considering the half-life of approximately 12 h for glargine insulin and 5–6 h for detemir insulin, along with the fact that endogenous insulin secretion is higher after meals, the influence of basal insulin on postprandial 2-h INS2h/PBG or CP2h/PBG levels should be minimal.

In summary, we hypothesize that the primary mechanisms through which long-acting insulin affects fasting insulin and C-peptide levels in persons with diabetes are as follows. In the physiological state, elevated blood glucose levels are transported into β cells through Glut-2. Through the process of glycolysis, adenosine triphosphate (ATP) is produced, which inhibits potassium ion (K +) channels. This, in turn, causes INS granules to fuse with the pancreatic cell membrane, releasing INS and CP (proinsulin produced by β cells is broken down into equal amounts of INS and CP into the bloodstream). As exogenous insulin is used, blood glucose levels decrease, and the amount of INS and CP released into the bloodstream also decreases. As a result, the level of CP detected in the blood decreases. Detemir insulin cannot be detected by electrochemiluminescence, so plasma insulin levels are reduced. On the other hand, glargine insulin can be detected by electrochemiluminescence, so plasma insulin levels approximate those observed in the physiological state. In clinical practice, it is crucial to recognize that relying solely on fasting C-peptide levels to evaluate basal pancreatic β-cell function in diabetes patients using basal insulins, such as glargine insulin and detemir insulin, may lead to an underestimation of pancreatic function. Therefore, when assessing fasting insulin levels, it is essential to consider the specific insulin types and detection methods employed. Specifically, if the ECLIA method is utilized for testing, patients who have used glargine insulin the night before can directly assess their pancreatic function based on their fasting insulin levels. However, the use of detemir insulin may potentially yield underestimated results. To address this concern, we have conducted preliminary calculations to develop a regression equation that incorporates fasting C-peptide and insulin levels from patients receiving insulin treatment. This equation aims to estimate the true levels in individuals who do not use INS. It is noteworthy that the regression equation demonstrated the strongest correlation with fasting insulin levels in both patients treated with glargine insulin and those who remained untreated. Nevertheless, it is crucial to emphasize that the equation’s application is currently limited due to the inclusion of a small number of cases and the absence of further clinical validation. The areas under the ROC curves for predicting true CP levels after treatment with glargine and detemir were 0.7768 and 0.8762, respectively (P < 0.001), with cutoff values of 0.4435 nmol/L (sensitivity 52.2%; specificity 93.3%) and 0.379 nmol/L (sensitivity 86.4%; specificity 76.8%). This suggests that post-treatment CP levels can be used to predict true fasting C-peptide level abnormalities. Fasting C-peptide levels below 0.4435 nmol/L or 0.379 nmol/L under glargine and detemir treatment, respectively, indicate lower than normal true fasting C-peptide levels, suggesting poorer pancreatic function in patients.

The current study has some limitations. First, we were not able to evaluate all types of exogenous insulins due to their relatively early initiation. It is worth noting that detemir insulin and glargine insulin remain clinically relevant in certain regions of China. Meanwhile, we have applied to expand the research scope to investigate the impact of currently mainstream exogenous insulin formulations on endogenous insulin detection. Second, the sample size was small, so additional data from more patients are needed to verify the results. Lastly, the hyperinsulinemic-euglycemic clamping test is the superior method by which to evaluate islet β-cell function, which was not used in this study.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: The levels of fasting C-peptide and insulin after the use of detemir insulin were lower than the actual hormone levels. After administration of glargine insulin, fasting C-peptide levels decreased, and detected fasting insulin levels reflected actual insulin levels. Therefore, for the patients who used glargine insulin the night before, their true basal islet function could be judged based on their fasting insulin test levels, whereas administration of detemir insulin the night before resulted in an underestimation of the patients’ true basal islet function. Therefore, it is not accurate to solely rely on CP levels as the sole determinant for directly assessing pancreatic function in diabetes patients who are undergoing basal insulin therapy. It is imperative to take into account the specific type of INS being administered and the methodologies employed for measuring both INS and CP levels in order to achieve a comprehensive evaluation.
